questions.question: What are the different states in a Java thread lifecycle?
questions.title: Java Thread Lifecycle States
questions.direct_answer: Java threads have 6 states defined in `Thread.State`: **NEW** (created, not started), **RUNNABLE** (running or ready to run), **BLOCKED** (waiting for a lock), **WAITING** (indefinitely waiting), **TIMED_WAITING** (waiting with timeout), and **TERMINATED** (finished).

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to name and describe each lifecycle state — often drawn on a whiteboard
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing BLOCKED and WAITING — they're different things
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain what causes each transition, not just list the state names

sections.title: Thread States and Transitions
sections.content:
| State | Description | Caused by |
|---|---|---|
| NEW | Thread created, not yet started | new Thread() |
| RUNNABLE | Running or ready to run | start() called |
| BLOCKED | Waiting to acquire a monitor lock | Another thread holds the lock |
| WAITING | Indefinitely waiting for signal | wait(), join(), LockSupport.park() |
| TIMED_WAITING | Waiting with timeout | sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms) |
| TERMINATED | Execution completed | run() returned or threw exception |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- NEW → RUNNABLE: thread.start()
- RUNNABLE → BLOCKED: trying to enter synchronized block held by another thread
- RUNNABLE → WAITING: calling wait() or join() without timeout
- RUNNABLE → TIMED_WAITING: sleep(ms), wait(ms), or join(ms)
- WAITING/TIMED_WAITING → RUNNABLE: notify(), notifyAll(), timeout expires, join completes
- BLOCKED → RUNNABLE: lock becomes available
- RUNNABLE → TERMINATED: run() completes or throws

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Java threads have six states. NEW is when you create a Thread object but haven't called start() yet. RUNNABLE means the thread is either running on a CPU or ready to run and waiting for CPU time — Java combines these. BLOCKED is specifically when the thread is waiting to acquire a synchronized lock that another thread is holding. WAITING is when the thread is waiting indefinitely for another thread to do something, like calling wait() or join(). TIMED_WAITING is similar but with a timeout — like sleep(1000) or wait(1000). TERMINATED means run() finished. The important distinction is BLOCKED vs WAITING — BLOCKED is always about acquiring a lock, WAITING is about coordinating with another thread.

beats.text: A Java thread moves through 6 states defined in Thread.State: NEW (created, not started), RUNNABLE (running or ready), BLOCKED (waiting for a lock), WAITING (waiting indefinitely for a signal), TIMED_WAITING (waiting with a timeout), and TERMINATED (done).

Threads don't just run continuously. They pause for locks, wait for conditions, or sleep. Understanding states helps you read thread dumps, diagnose deadlocks, and understand why a thread isn't making progress.

items: NEW: Thread object created, start() not called yet.
RUNNABLE: Running on a CPU or queued and ready — Java combines these into one state.
BLOCKED: Wants to enter a synchronized block but another thread holds the lock.
WAITING: Called wait() or join() with no timeout — waiting for a signal.
TIMED_WAITING: Called sleep(ms), wait(ms), or join(ms) — has a timeout.
TERMINATED: run() returned or threw an uncaught exception.

beats.text: candidates miss: BLOCKED and WAITING both mean 'not running' but they're completely different. BLOCKED means passively stuck at a synchronized door. WAITING means you deliberately called wait() and released the lock, waiting for someone to call notify(). A thread dump shows the difference — BLOCKED threads show 'waiting to lock', WAITING threads show 'Object.wait()'.

items: Confusing BLOCKED with WAITING — BLOCKED is about a lock, WAITING is about a condition signal.
RUNNABLE doesn't mean the thread is actually running right now — it might be waiting for CPU time.

questions.question: What is the difference between BLOCKED and WAITING state in Java threads?
questions.title: BLOCKED vs WAITING Thread State
questions.direct_answer: **BLOCKED** means waiting to acquire a **synchronized lock** held by another thread. **WAITING** means the thread voluntarily paused and is waiting for another thread to signal it via `notify()` or `notifyAll()`. Both are not running, but the cause and resolution are different.

interviewer_intent.testing: Nuanced understanding — many freshers confuse these two
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the mechanism: BLOCKED is passive, WAITING is cooperative/voluntary

sections.title: BLOCKED vs WAITING
sections.content:
| Aspect | BLOCKED | WAITING |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting for | A lock (monitor) | A notification/signal |
| Triggered by | Trying to enter synchronized block | Calling wait(), join() |
| Woken up by | Lock becomes available | notify(), notifyAll(), join completes |
| Lock held? | Doesn't hold the lock it needs | Releases lock while waiting (wait()) |
| Interrupt response | Cannot be interrupted | Can be interrupted (InterruptedException) |
| In thread dump | at ... (waiting for lock) | ... in Object.wait() |

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: BLOCKED and WAITING are both 'not running' states but for completely different reasons. BLOCKED happens when a thread tries to enter a synchronized block but another thread already holds that lock — it's just waiting passively at the door. WAITING happens when a thread calls wait() on an object inside a synchronized block — it voluntarily releases the lock and waits for another thread to call notify(). The key difference: BLOCKED can't do anything until the lock is released by someone else. WAITING is intentional — the thread is participating in coordination with another thread and will be woken up explicitly. In a thread dump, you can see BLOCKED threads show 'waiting to lock' while WAITING threads show 'Object.wait()'.

groups.heading: BLOCKED
groups.text: A thread enters BLOCKED when it tries to enter a synchronized block but another thread already holds that lock. It's passive — just waiting at the door. It becomes RUNNABLE automatically when the lock is released.

groups.heading: WAITING
groups.text: A thread enters WAITING by voluntarily calling wait() inside a synchronized block. It releases the lock and waits for another thread to call notify() or notifyAll(). It's cooperative — it's actively participating in a coordination protocol.

values: Doesn't have the lock it needs

items: In thread dumps, look for 'waiting to lock' for BLOCKED threads and 'Object.wait()' for WAITING threads.

questions.question: What is Thread.join() and when would you use it?
questions.title: Thread.join() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `Thread.join()` makes the **current thread wait** until the thread it's called on **terminates**. It's used to ensure a thread has completed before the caller proceeds — for example, waiting for all worker threads to finish before aggregating results.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the timeout version join(ms) and show a practical use case with multiple threads

sections.title: Thread.join() Example
Key Points
sections.content:
- join() causes the calling thread to enter WAITING state
- join(milliseconds) — timeout version; calling thread continues after timeout even if not done
- join() throws InterruptedException — must be handled
- Equivalent to 'wait for thread to reach TERMINATED state'
- Use case: fan-out/fan-in pattern — start multiple workers, join all before combining results
- Main thread commonly joins worker threads before printing final results

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: join() is how you make one thread wait for another to finish. If you call workerThread.join() from the main thread, the main thread pauses and waits until the worker thread terminates. A practical use case: you split a computation across 4 worker threads, start them all, then call join() on each one. After all joins complete, you know all workers are done and can safely aggregate the results. join() throws InterruptedException, so you need to handle that. There's also a join(milliseconds) version that has a timeout — if the thread doesn't finish in time, join() returns anyway.

beats.text: Calling workerThread.join() from the current thread makes the current thread pause and wait until workerThread terminates. The current thread enters WAITING state until the worker is done. join(ms) adds a timeout — the current thread continues after that many milliseconds even if the worker isn't finished.
Without join(), you have no reliable way to know when a thread has finished. You'd need shared flags and volatile variables. join() gives you a clean, blocking way to wait for completion.

items: join() with no args: current thread waits indefinitely until the target thread terminates.
join(ms): current thread waits at most ms milliseconds, then continues regardless.
join() throws InterruptedException — must be handled in a try-catch.

beats.text: non-obvious: join() on a thread that hasn't started yet — or one that's already terminated — returns immediately. It doesn't throw. So calling join() before start() is a silent no-op, which can make code look correct when it isn't.

items: Calling join() on a thread that hasn't started is a silent no-op — the code continues immediately.
For managing many threads, ExecutorService.awaitTermination() is cleaner than join()-ing each one manually.

speakable_v2.cap: join() is the thread equivalent of 'wait for them to finish before we continue' — straightforward but watch for InterruptedException.

questions.question: What does Thread.yield() do?
questions.title: Thread.yield() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `Thread.yield()` is a **hint** to the JVM scheduler that the current thread is willing to give up CPU time and let other threads run. The scheduler may or may not honor this hint — the behavior is implementation-dependent and rarely used in production code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Breadth of threading knowledge — not commonly used but sometimes asked
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking yield() guarantees another thread runs next
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast with sleep(0) and explain why yield() is rarely useful in practice

sections.title: Thread.yield() Explained
sections.content:
`Thread.yield()` moves the current thread from RUNNING to RUNNABLE, hinting that the scheduler should pick another thread of the **same or higher priority**. However:

1. The scheduler may ignore the hint entirely
2. The same thread may be selected to run again immediately
3. Behavior varies across JVMs and operating systems

In practice, `yield()` is almost never used in real applications. It was more relevant in old cooperative multitasking environments. Modern JVM schedulers handle thread time slicing automatically.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Thread.yield() is a hint to the scheduler that the current thread is willing to give up CPU time. The thread moves to the RUNNABLE state — not BLOCKED or WAITING — and the scheduler decides what to run next. The key word is 'hint': the scheduler can completely ignore it, and the same thread might keep running. In practice, yield() is almost never used in production code. Modern JVM schedulers handle thread scheduling automatically. I'd say if you find yourself reaching for yield() to fix a concurrency problem, there's probably a better solution involving proper synchronization.

In early cooperative multitasking systems, threads had to explicitly yield to let others run. Modern JVMs use preemptive scheduling — they slice CPU time automatically. yield() is mostly a historical artifact.

questions.question: What is thread priority in Java and does it matter?
questions.title: Thread Priority in Java
questions.direct_answer: Java threads have a **priority** from 1 (MIN_PRIORITY) to 10 (MAX_PRIORITY), with 5 as default (NORM_PRIORITY). Higher-priority threads are **more likely** to be scheduled, but JVM thread scheduling is **platform-dependent** — priority is a hint, not a guarantee.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic thread knowledge — priority is often asked but rarely relied upon
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking thread priority guarantees execution order
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain platform dependency and why production code should not rely on thread priorities

sections.title: Thread Priority Example
Key Points
sections.content:
- Priority range: 1 (MIN_PRIORITY) to 10 (MAX_PRIORITY), default is 5 (NORM_PRIORITY)
- Set with thread.setPriority(n), get with thread.getPriority()
- Higher priority threads get more CPU time — on average, not guaranteed
- Priority inheritance: new threads inherit priority from their creating thread
- Platform-dependent: Linux may not honor priorities the same way as Windows
- Production code should NOT rely on priority for correctness

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Java threads have priorities from 1 to 10, where 5 is the default. You can set priority with thread.setPriority(). In theory, higher-priority threads are more likely to be scheduled. In practice, thread scheduling is platform-dependent — on Linux, for example, JVM thread priorities don't map cleanly to OS thread priorities. The key point is that priority is a hint, not a guarantee. You should never write code where correctness depends on thread priority ordering. If you need a specific execution order, use proper synchronization mechanisms.

questions.question: How can you stop a thread in Java? Is Thread.stop() safe?
questions.title: Stopping Threads Safely in Java
questions.direct_answer: `Thread.stop()` is **deprecated and unsafe** — it forcefully kills the thread, potentially leaving shared objects in an inconsistent state. The safe way to stop a thread is using a **volatile boolean flag** that the thread periodically checks, or using **Thread.interrupt()**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of cooperative thread cancellation — important for production code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Thread.stop() is deprecated and dangerous
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the volatile flag pattern and explain why it's cooperative/safe

sections.title: Safe Thread Stopping with Volatile Flag
Why Thread.stop() is Dangerous
sections.content:
Thread.stop() throws a `ThreadDeath` error at any arbitrary point in the thread's execution — even in the middle of synchronized blocks or object modifications. This can leave shared data in an inconsistent state, corrupting your data structures.

The safe alternatives:
1. **Volatile flag** — thread checks a boolean flag and exits cleanly
2. **Thread.interrupt()** — sets the interrupted flag; code must check Thread.interrupted() or catch InterruptedException
3. **Future.cancel(true)** — if using ExecutorService

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Thread.stop() is deprecated because it's dangerous — it forcefully throws a ThreadDeath error at whatever point the thread is executing, even if it's in the middle of updating a shared data structure. That can leave your objects in a corrupted state. The safe approach is cooperative cancellation: use a volatile boolean flag that the thread checks periodically. When you want to stop the thread, set the flag to false and the thread will exit its loop cleanly at a safe point. Thread.interrupt() is another option — it sets the interrupted flag, and the thread can check it or rely on InterruptedException from sleep() and wait() calls.
